screens.title: Optimizing Query Performance
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll focus on practical techniques that make Snowflake queries faster and less costly. You will learn how to use the EXPLAIN command to inspect execution plans, how to write queries that filter early and only select necessary columns, and when to consider clustering keys for very large tables. These ideas hang together: reducing bytes scanned and improving pruning reduces runtime and compute cost, while proper joins and projection minimize intermediate work. We’ll look at concrete S Q L examples you can run, show how to read partitions scanned and bytes scanned in EXPLAIN output, and point out common anti-patterns that often cause wasted work. By the end you’ll be able to run EXPLAIN on a slow query, identify the biggest contributors to work, and apply one or two targeted changes — filter by a prunable column, remove a SELECT * or reorder joins — to see a measurable improvement. Think of this as a diagnosis workflow: measure with EXPLAIN, change a single thing, re-measure, and decide whether larger steps like clustering or warehouse scaling are warranted.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Optimizing Query Performance
Optimizing Query Performance
Measure with EXPLAIN, reduce scanned data, and apply best-practice SQL to control cost.
In this lesson
You will learn to run EXPLAIN, interpret partitions and bytes scanned, and apply filters, projection, and clustering wisely to reduce compute.

Faster queries save time and reduce virtual warehouse cost. Small SQL changes often have outsized effects on bytes scanned.
Explore Key Topics

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives set a practical roadmap. First, you'll learn to use the EXPLAIN command to generate an execution plan without running the query, so you can observe partitions scanned and bytes scanned and detect the heaviest operations. Second, you'll learn concrete S Q L patterns: filtering early, selecting only needed columns, and structuring joins so Snowflake's optimizer has smaller intermediate datasets to work on. Third, you'll understand micro-partitions and how pruning uses min/max metadata to skip irrelevant data — this is fundamental to reducing read volume. Fourth, you'll learn when and how to use clustering keys for very large tables and the cost trade-offs around manual or automatic reclustering. Each objective points to a measurable action: run EXPLAIN, rewrite a query to filter earlier, review partitions scanned, and consider clustering only when the benefits exceed reclustering cost. These are practical, repeatable skills you can apply to real queries to reduce runtime and cloud cost.

screens.title: EXPLAIN: Generate an execution plan
screens.narratorSegment: The EXPLAIN command is your primary diagnostic tool for query performance in Snowflake. It produces an execution plan that lists the operations Snowflake will take — scans, joins, aggregations — without actually running the query. Practically, this means you can see which steps would read the most bytes or scan the most micro-partitions before you consume compute credits. A useful workflow is to prefix your slow query with EXPLAIN and look specifically at partitions scanned and bytes scanned in the output. If a scan reports very large bytes or many partitions, focus on reducing that scan first. For example, if WHERE filters are missing or placed after aggregation, huge scans can happen. A concrete example from the chapter shows EXPLAIN for a customer spend query that joins customers and orders; you should inspect whether the orders scan dominates and whether adding a date filter reduces partitions scanned. A common misconception is that EXPLAIN is only for tuning complex queries — even simple SELECTs benefit, because EXPLAIN surfaces hidden large scans. Try this on a query you run often, and ask: which operation reads the most data? That becomes your optimization target.

keyIdea.title: Diagnose before changing
keyIdea.text: Run EXPLAIN to see which operations scan the most data and use that to prioritize fixes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › EXPLAIN: Generate an execution plan
Code Example
EXPLAIN
SELECT
  c.customer_name,
  SUM(o.order_total) AS total_spent
FROM
  customers c
JOIN
  orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE
  o.order_date >= '2023-01-01'
GROUP BY
  c.customer_name
ORDER BY
  total_spent DESC
LIMIT 10;
Prefixing EXPLAIN prevents execution but shows steps and metrics like partitions scanned and bytes scanned. Use these numbers to find the largest scans.
How to read EXPLAIN
  • Find operations with the largest bytes scanned — they are primary targets.
  • Look for scans on wide tables or joins that lack filters; those often cause high read volume.
  • Compare EXPLAIN before and after a single SQL change to measure impact on partitions scanned.
Example
On a customer-orders join, adding a date filter on orders often reduces partitions scanned significantly because date is prunable.
Common Mistake
Assuming an optimizer will always fix a bad query. EXPLAIN reveals where automatic optimization can’t avoid large scans.
Key Takeaway
EXPLAIN is inexpensive and informative; start every performance investigation with it.

screens.title: Interpreting EXPLAIN output
screens.narratorSegment: Interpreting EXPLAIN output is a simple triage process: locate the largest scans, form a minimal change to reduce them, and re-run EXPLAIN to confirm impact. Begin by scanning the plan and identifying steps that report high partitions scanned or bytes scanned. These steps frequently correspond to a full table scan, an unfiltered join, or an expensive aggregation. Next, ask what can be filtered before that step. Common answers are date ranges, region codes, or other columns with strong correlation to micro-partitions. Implement one targeted change — for example, add a WHERE on sale_date — and re-run EXPLAIN to measure reduction. Beware a common misconception: not every reduction in elapsed time requires a clustering key. Small S Q L changes often cut scanned bytes dramatically. Use EXPLAIN numbers as objective evidence: if partitions scanned drop by orders of magnitude, you have a clear win. If not, then consider structural options like clustering or a different join approach. This measurement-first process reduces guesswork and keeps optimization cost-effective. Interpreting EXPLAIN output means identify expensive scans, make one focused change, and re-measure to decide the next step.. In practical terms, focus on partitions scanned and bytes scanned to prioritize fixes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Interpreting EXPLAIN output
Triage Steps
  1. Locate heavy scans: find steps with large bytes or partitions scanned.
  2. Ask what can be pruned: is there a date or categorical filter you can add?
  3. Change one thing: add or move a WHERE, project fewer columns, or reorder joins.
  4. Re-run EXPLAIN: confirm partitions and bytes scanned decreased.
Pro Tip
Small, measurable changes avoid unnecessary work. Use EXPLAIN numbers as your objective metric.
Example comparison
Before
No date filter: partitions scanned = many, bytes scanned = large. Join scans full orders table.
After
Add WHERE sale_date >= '2023-01-01', partitions scanned drops and bytes scanned falls dramatically.
Key Takeaway

Use EXPLAIN's numbers as the decision basis for choosing SQL changes over structural ones like clustering.

screens.title: Filter Early: Before vs After
screens.narratorSegment: Filtering early is one of the simplest but most powerful optimizations. When you apply WHERE conditions before joins or aggregations, you reduce the size of intermediate results and the amount of data Snowflake must process. Consider two patterns: one that groups first and filters later, and one that filters in the WHERE clause before aggregation. The grouped-then-filtered pattern forces aggregation over a larger dataset and may scan many micro-partitions unnecessarily. The correct approach is to push selective predicates down so the engine processes less data. A concrete example from the chapter contrasts a query that uses HAVING to filter a category after aggregation with a query that uses WHERE to filter the category first. The WHERE version typically scans far fewer rows, shrinks intermediate results, and lowers bytes scanned shown by EXPLAIN. A common misconception is that the optimizer will always reorder filters for you; while Snowflake is smart, writing clear, early filters is a reliable way to reduce work and ensure consistent performance. Filter Early: Before vs After means apply where predicates before joins and aggregation so the engine processes less data and scans fewer partitions.. In practical terms, why applying where clauses before joins and aggregations matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Push filters down
keyIdea.text: Apply WHERE predicates before joins and aggregation so the engine processes less data and scans fewer partitions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Filter Early: Before vs After
Bad pattern
SELECT
  product_category,
  SUM(sales_amount) AS total_sales
FROM
  sales
GROUP BY
  product_category
HAVING
  product_category = 'Electronics';
This groups the full table then filters, causing aggregation on all data and higher scanned bytes.
Good pattern
SELECT
  product_category,
  SUM(sales_amount) AS total_sales
FROM
  sales
WHERE
  product_category = 'Electronics'
GROUP BY
  product_category;
Filtering first reduces rows passed to aggregation, often reducing partitions scanned and runtime.
Analogy
Sort mail by destination before sorting for delivery routes — fewer items to route saves time.
Misconception
Assuming the optimizer will always reorder filtering. Explicit early filters are safer and clearer.
Key Takeaway
Applying filters early reduces intermediate data and often lowers bytes scanned dramatically.

screens.title: Select necessary columns
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting only the columns you need is a straightforward optimization that reduces data transferred and the work Snowflake must do. SELECT * forces Snowflake to read all columns, including wide or large types that may not be required downstream. On wide tables, unnecessary columns can significantly increase bytes scanned even if your WHERE is selective. The practical rule is to list required columns explicitly in production queries, especially in ETL and reporting jobs. A concrete example in the chapter compares SELECT * on a large customer table filtered by region with a focused SELECT of customer_id, customer_name, and email. The focused query scans and transfers less data, lowers compute usage, and often improves query planning. A common misconception is that SELECT * is harmless for small ad-hoc queries; while okay for quick exploration, it habitually leaks into production and causes persistent cost and performance issues. Make column projection a standard code review and automation rule. Select necessary columns means explicit column lists reduce scanned data and make intentions clear to the optimizer and reviewers.. In practical terms, avoid select * to reduce data transferred and processed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Select necessary columns
Anti-pattern
-- Bad
SELECT * FROM large_customer_table WHERE region = 'EMEA';
This reads all columns for matching rows, increasing bytes scanned and downstream data movement.
Best practice
-- Good
SELECT customer_id, customer_name, email
FROM large_customer_table
WHERE region = 'EMEA';
Projection reduces what must be read and transferred. It also makes intent explicit for code reviewers.
When SELECT * is acceptable
Ad-hoc exploration or quick debugging, but avoid in scheduled jobs and shared views.
Key Takeaway
Be explicit about columns in production to shrink scanned bytes and save credits.

screens.title: Join optimization
screens.narratorSegment: Join behavior influences the size of intermediate results and the amount of data scanned. Snowflake’s optimizer is powerful, but it still benefits from logical join order and efficient join conditions. The general guideline is to apply selective filters to tables before joining and, when possible, join smaller filtered tables first so the engine doesn’t produce a massive intermediate set. Also ensure join columns share compatible data types and that joins are on keys when possible — joining on mismatched or high-cardinality non-key columns can multiply work. A concrete scenario: joining a filtered orders subset to a customers table will usually be cheaper than joining full orders and customers and then filtering. A common misconception is to rely solely on hints or manual reordering; start by ensuring your predicates reduce the larger table early. When a query still scans too much data after these changes, consider restructuring the query or using intermediate temporary tables to materialize filtered subsets. These steps keep intermediate work small and often produce immediate EXPLAIN improvements. Join optimization means filter large tables before joining and prefer joins on keys with compatible types to minimize intermediate data.. In practical terms, order joins, use keys, and reduce intermediate result size. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Join optimization
Rules of thumb
  • Filter large tables before joining to reduce rows participating in the join.
  • Join smaller, filtered tables first to keep intermediates small.
  • Ensure join columns use compatible data types and are appropriate keys.
Scenario
If orders is much larger than customers, filter orders by date first, then join to customers to reduce the join footprint.
Quick fixes
Materialize filtered sets
Use temporary tables for very large filters to avoid repeated scanning during complex joins.
Avoid non-key joins
Joining on high-cardinality non-key columns can blow up intermediate sizes.
Key Takeaway
Reduce the amount of data participating in joins by filtering and ordering joins logically before escalating to structural changes.

screens.title: Micro-partitions and pruning
screens.narratorSegment: Micro-partitions are Snowflake’s basic storage unit, typically ranging from about 50 to 500 megabytes compressed. Each micro-partition stores metadata such as min and max values for columns. Snowflake uses this metadata to perform pruning: if a query’s filters fall entirely outside a micro-partition’s min/max ranges, Snowflake skips that micro-partition entirely. This is the core mechanism that makes selective queries fast and inexpensive. For example, if a table is organized by sale_date and your WHERE clause filters to a narrow date range, pruning can skip many micro-partitions and dramatically reduce bytes scanned. A misconception is that micro-partitions are the same as user-created partitions — they are managed automatically by Snowflake. Understanding micro-partition pruning helps you choose which columns to filter on and whether clustering keys might further improve pruning for very large tables. The goal is to write queries and design data layouts that align with pruning so Snowflake can skip work instead of doing it. Micro-partitions and pruning means filters that align with micro-partition min/max metadata let snowflake skip many micro-partitions and save bytes scanned.. In practical terms, how snowflake skips irrelevant data using micro-partition metadata. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Filters that align with micro-partition min/max metadata let Snowflake skip many micro-partitions and save bytes scanned.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Micro-partitions and pruning
What are micro-partitions?
Snowflake automatically stores table data in consecutive micro-partitions. Each micro-partition carries metadata such as min/max per column. This metadata is cheap to consult and powers pruning.
Why it matters
When your filters align with micro-partition ranges, Snowflake can skip scanning entire micro-partitions and avoid reading bytes.
Pruning example
If sale_date column's micro-partition ranges do not overlap your requested date range, Snowflake prunes those partitions and does not read them. This is the core reason why filtering on date often reduces scanned bytes drastically.
Misconception
Micro-partitions are not user-managed; they are Snowflake-managed units. Clustering only adjusts how rows with similar values are co-located across micro-partitions.
Key Takeaway
Design queries to filter on columns with strong micro-partition correlation to allow pruning to skip work.

screens.title: Clustering keys and reclustering
screens.narratorSegment: Clustering keys tell Snowflake which column or columns should be co-located across micro-partitions so that rows with similar values end up together. This can improve pruning for very large tables where correlations exist between a queried column and table storage layout. However, clustering is not free: reclustering requires credits and can be automatic or manual. Use clustering keys selectively on multiple-terabyte tables with frequent range scans or filters on the clustering columns. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Clustering keys and reclustering
What clustering does
Clustering arranges data so similar values of specified columns are co-located in the same micro-partitions, improving pruning for range queries and correlated filters on very large tables.
Commands
ALTER TABLE sales_data CLUSTER BY (order_date, product_id); ALTER TABLE sales_data RECLUSTER;
Trade-offs
  • Benefit: improved pruning and fewer partitions scanned for targeted queries.
  • Cost: reclustering consumes credits; automatic clustering may add sustained cost.
  • When to use: high-volume tables with repeated queries on correlated columns.
Key Takeaway
Only adopt clustering after EXPLAIN shows persistent large scans on correlated columns and when the expected pruning gain justifies reclustering cost.

screens.title: Anti-patterns that slow queries
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter lists several anti-patterns that commonly cause poor performance and higher cost. First, overusing SELECT * reads all columns unnecessarily and increases bytes scanned. Second, complex subqueries or CTEs that are not optimized can force repeated scans or inefficient plans; sometimes breaking logic into simpler steps or temporary tables helps. Third, inefficient join conditions — for example joining on non-key or mismatched data types — can blow up intermediate results. Fourth, sorting a massive dataset before filtering with ORDER BY and LIMIT is wasteful; always filter first, then sort the reduced set if possible. Fifth, not leveraging result caching for repeated identical queries causes avoidable compute. Finally, choosing an undersized virtual warehouse for heavy workloads can increase run time and cost; a warehouse that is too small will lengthen execution and may incur more credits. Recognizing these patterns early helps you prioritize inexpensive S Q L changes before scaling or structural adjustments. Anti-patterns that slow queries means eliminate select *, push filters early, fix joins, and use caching; scale warehouses only after sql improvements.. In practical terms, recognize and avoid the patterns that increase scanned data or runtime. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Result caching and warehouse sizing
screens.narratorSegment: Result caching can offer large savings for repetitive queries on static or infrequently changing data. Snowflake returns cached results when a subsequent query is identical to a prior one and the underlying data hasn't changed. Small changes to the query text or use of non-deterministic functions will invalidate the cache. Use this knowledge for reporting queries that run unchanged: schedule identical queries or reuse identical S Q L to take advantage of cached results. Warehouse sizing is a separate consideration. Increasing warehouse size can reduce elapsed time for C P U-bound operations, but it also increases per-second credit consumption. An undersized warehouse may run longer and accumulate similar or higher total cost. The practical approach is to first reduce scanned bytes and optimize S Q L; only then scale the warehouse to improve latency. A common misconception is that bigger warehouses always save money — they only help when the workload benefits from additional parallelism and you've eliminated unnecessary reads. Result caching and warehouse sizing means use result cache where possible for repeated identical queries and choose warehouse size after sql optimizations.. In practical terms, leverage caching and match warehouse size to workload. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Result caching and warehouse sizing
Result cache
If a query is identical to a prior run and the underlying data hasn't changed, Snowflake may return cached results without running the plan. Keep queries stable when you want caching benefits. Avoid non-deterministic functions when caching is desired.
When it helps
Repeated reports and dashboards on static snapshots benefit the most from result caching.
Warehouse sizing
Choose a warehouse size after optimizing SQL. Larger warehouses increase parallelism but also seconds-per-credit. Test whether your workload is I/O bound or compute bound before deciding to scale up.
Misconception
Bigger warehouses always save money. Not necessarily — if queries waste time scanning data, scaling will only cost more.
Key Takeaway
Use result cache for repeated identical queries and reserve warehouse scaling for when SQL and pruning are already optimized.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll focus on practical techniques that make Snowflake queries faster and less costly. You will learn how to use the EXPLAIN command to inspect execution plans, how to write queries that filter early and only select necessary columns, and when to consider clustering keys for very large tables. These ideas hang together: reducing bytes scanned and improving pruning reduces runtime and compute cost, while proper joins and projection minimize intermediate work. We’ll look at concrete S Q L examples you can run, show how to read partitions scanned and bytes scanned in EXPLAIN output, and point out common anti-patterns that often cause wasted work. By the end you’ll be able to run EXPLAIN on a slow query, identify the biggest contributors to work, and apply one or two targeted changes — filter by a prunable column, remove a SELECT * or reorder joins — to see a measurable improvement. Think of this as a diagnosis workflow: measure with EXPLAIN, change a single thing, re-measure, and decide whether larger steps like clustering or warehouse scaling are warranted.

These four objectives set a practical roadmap. First, you'll learn to use the EXPLAIN command to generate an execution plan without running the query, so you can observe partitions scanned and bytes scanned and detect the heaviest operations. Second, you'll learn concrete S Q L patterns: filtering early, selecting only needed columns, and structuring joins so Snowflake's optimizer has smaller intermediate datasets to work on. Third, you'll understand micro-partitions and how pruning uses min/max metadata to skip irrelevant data — this is fundamental to reducing read volume. Fourth, you'll learn when and how to use clustering keys for very large tables and the cost trade-offs around manual or automatic reclustering. Each objective points to a measurable action: run EXPLAIN, rewrite a query to filter earlier, review partitions scanned, and consider clustering only when the benefits exceed reclustering cost. These are practical, repeatable skills you can apply to real queries to reduce runtime and cloud cost.

This continuation drills into operational skills that complement the four core objectives. First, you'll learn to reduce data scanned by applying targeted filters on prunable columns such as dates or partition-like keys. Second, you'll practice avoiding anti-patterns like overusing SELECT * and sorting huge results before filtering, both of which increase work and cost. Third, you will learn to interpret EXPLAIN metrics like partitions scanned and bytes scanned and use those numbers to decide whether to change S Q L or adjust clustering. Fourth, you'll monitor warehouse usage and match virtual warehouse size to workload — an undersized warehouse can lengthen runs and increase overall cost because queries run longer. Together these behaviours form a workflow: measure with EXPLAIN, change S Q L to reduce scanned bytes, re-run EXPLAIN, then consider operational options like clustering or resizing. The goal is repeatable, observable improvement on real queries.

The EXPLAIN command is your primary diagnostic tool for query performance in Snowflake. It produces an execution plan that lists the operations Snowflake will take — scans, joins, aggregations — without actually running the query. Practically, this means you can see which steps would read the most bytes or scan the most micro-partitions before you consume compute credits. A useful workflow is to prefix your slow query with EXPLAIN and look specifically at partitions scanned and bytes scanned in the output. If a scan reports very large bytes or many partitions, focus on reducing that scan first. For example, if WHERE filters are missing or placed after aggregation, huge scans can happen. A concrete example from the chapter shows EXPLAIN for a customer spend query that joins customers and orders; you should inspect whether the orders scan dominates and whether adding a date filter reduces partitions scanned. A common misconception is that EXPLAIN is only for tuning complex queries — even simple SELECTs benefit, because EXPLAIN surfaces hidden large scans. Try this on a query you run often, and ask: which operation reads the most data? That becomes your optimization target.

Interpreting EXPLAIN output is a simple triage process: locate the largest scans, form a minimal change to reduce them, and re-run EXPLAIN to confirm impact. Begin by scanning the plan and identifying steps that report high partitions scanned or bytes scanned. These steps frequently correspond to a full table scan, an unfiltered join, or an expensive aggregation. Next, ask what can be filtered before that step. Common answers are date ranges, region codes, or other columns with strong correlation to micro-partitions. Implement one targeted change — for example, add a WHERE on sale_date — and re-run EXPLAIN to measure reduction. Beware a common misconception: not every reduction in elapsed time requires a clustering key. Small S Q L changes often cut scanned bytes dramatically. Use EXPLAIN numbers as objective evidence: if partitions scanned drop by orders of magnitude, you have a clear win. If not, then consider structural options like clustering or a different join approach. This measurement-first process reduces guesswork and keeps optimization cost-effective. Interpreting EXPLAIN output means identify expensive scans, make one focused change, and re-measure to decide the next step.. In practical terms, focus on partitions scanned and bytes scanned to prioritize fixes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Filtering early is one of the simplest but most powerful optimizations. When you apply WHERE conditions before joins or aggregations, you reduce the size of intermediate results and the amount of data Snowflake must process. Consider two patterns: one that groups first and filters later, and one that filters in the WHERE clause before aggregation. The grouped-then-filtered pattern forces aggregation over a larger dataset and may scan many micro-partitions unnecessarily. The correct approach is to push selective predicates down so the engine processes less data. A concrete example from the chapter contrasts a query that uses HAVING to filter a category after aggregation with a query that uses WHERE to filter the category first. The WHERE version typically scans far fewer rows, shrinks intermediate results, and lowers bytes scanned shown by EXPLAIN. A common misconception is that the optimizer will always reorder filters for you; while Snowflake is smart, writing clear, early filters is a reliable way to reduce work and ensure consistent performance. Filter Early: Before vs After means apply where predicates before joins and aggregation so the engine processes less data and scans fewer partitions.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Selecting only the columns you need is a straightforward optimization that reduces data transferred and the work Snowflake must do. SELECT * forces Snowflake to read all columns, including wide or large types that may not be required downstream. On wide tables, unnecessary columns can significantly increase bytes scanned even if your WHERE is selective. The practical rule is to list required columns explicitly in production queries, especially in ETL and reporting jobs. A concrete example in the chapter compares SELECT * on a large customer table filtered by region with a focused SELECT of customer_id, customer_name, and email. The focused query scans and transfers less data, lowers compute usage, and often improves query planning. A common misconception is that SELECT * is harmless for small ad-hoc queries; while okay for quick exploration, it habitually leaks into production and causes persistent cost and performance issues. Make column projection a standard code review and automation rule. Select necessary columns means explicit column lists reduce scanned data and make intentions clear to the optimizer and reviewers.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Join behavior influences the size of intermediate results and the amount of data scanned. Snowflake’s optimizer is powerful, but it still benefits from logical join order and efficient join conditions. The general guideline is to apply selective filters to tables before joining and, when possible, join smaller filtered tables first so the engine doesn’t produce a massive intermediate set. Also ensure join columns share compatible data types and that joins are on keys when possible — joining on mismatched or high-cardinality non-key columns can multiply work. A concrete scenario: joining a filtered orders subset to a customers table will usually be cheaper than joining full orders and customers and then filtering. A common misconception is to rely solely on hints or manual reordering; start by ensuring your predicates reduce the larger table early. When a query still scans too much data after these changes, consider restructuring the query or using intermediate temporary tables to materialize filtered subsets. These steps keep intermediate work small and often produce immediate EXPLAIN improvements. Join optimization means filter large tables before joining and prefer joins on keys with compatible types to minimize intermediate data.. Micro-partitions are Snowflake’s basic storage unit, typically ranging from about 50 to 500 megabytes compressed. Each micro-partition stores metadata such as min and max values for columns. Snowflake uses this metadata to perform pruning: if a query’s filters fall entirely outside a micro-partition’s min/max ranges, Snowflake skips that micro-partition entirely. This is the core mechanism that makes selective queries fast and inexpensive. For example, if a table is organized by sale_date and your WHERE clause filters to a narrow date range, pruning can skip many micro-partitions and dramatically reduce bytes scanned. A misconception is that micro-partitions are the same as user-created partitions — they are managed automatically by Snowflake. Understanding micro-partition pruning helps you choose which columns to filter on and whether clustering keys might further improve pruning for very large tables. The goal is to write queries and design data layouts that align with pruning so Snowflake can skip work instead of doing it. The chapter lists several anti-patterns that commonly cause poor performance and higher cost. First, overusing SELECT * reads all columns unnecessarily and increases bytes scanned. Second, complex subqueries or CTEs that are not optimized can force repeated scans or inefficient plans; sometimes breaking logic into simpler steps or temporary tables helps. Third, inefficient join conditions — for example joining on non-key or mismatched data types — can blow up intermediate results. Fourth, sorting a massive dataset before filtering with ORDER BY and LIMIT is wasteful; always filter first, then sort the reduced set if possible. Fifth, not leveraging result caching for repeated identical queries causes avoidable compute. Finally, choosing an undersized virtual warehouse for heavy workloads can increase run time and cost; a warehouse that is too small will lengthen execution and may incur more credits. Recognizing these patterns early helps you prioritize inexpensive S Q L changes before scaling or structural adjustments. Result caching can offer large savings for repetitive queries on static or infrequently changing data. Snowflake returns cached results when a subsequent query is identical to a prior one and the underlying data hasn't changed. Small changes to the query text or use of non-deterministic functions will invalidate the cache. Use this knowledge for reporting queries that run unchanged: schedule identical queries or reuse identical S Q L to take advantage of cached results. Warehouse sizing is a separate consideration. Increasing warehouse size can reduce elapsed time for C P U-bound operations, but it also increases per-second credit consumption. An undersized warehouse may run longer and accumulate similar or higher total cost. The practical approach is to first reduce scanned bytes and optimize S Q L; only then scale the warehouse to improve latency. A common misconception is that bigger warehouses always save money — they only help when the workload benefits from additional parallelism and you've eliminated unnecessary reads.
